display_title: Official Review of Paper2212 by Reviewer CaWn

content.summary_of_the_paper: Due to over-smoothing, Graph neural networks (GNNs) fail to prove the prediction performance by stacking layers. The frequency Principle demonstrates that deep neural networks fit target functions from low to high frequencies during the training. Based on these phenomena, the authors theoretically prove that low-frequency signals can be learned faster in GNNs because of the smoothness and low dimensionality. The authors also prove that adopting dropout on features prevents over-smoothing. Specifically, this paper proposes a Multi-Scale Frequency Enhanced Graph Neural Networks (MSF-GNNs), which decomposes signals into high-frequency and low-frequency components, uses mixed-order propagation rule and combines the supervised classification loss and the consistency regularization loss. Experiments are conducted on three benchmark datasets for node classification, showing the effectiveness of the proposed model.
content.main_review:
## Strength
I appreciate the motivation of this paper that GNNs learn low-frequency signals faster than high- frequency signals, thus designing models to fully exploit the advantages of different signals to mitigate over-smoothing is meaningful and insightful. 

## Weakness
1.	One of my major concerns is the novelty of this paper. As cited by the authors, Zheng et al. (2021) proposed a framelet-based graph convolution network and Berthelot et al. (2019) proposed the method of consistency regularization loss, the architecture of MSF-GNNs may not be novel and insightful enough. It is not clear what the main contribution of MSF-GNNs is.
2.	Since it is mentioned that low-frequency performs better in shallow layers, and high-frequency achieves higher accuracy in deep layers, the intuitive attempt is to design different message-passing rules to prevent over-smoothing in deep layers caused by low-frequency, while fully learning high- frequency information. But the proposed model does not deal with low-frequency and high-frequency separately. Instead, it uses the same update mechanism for two components.
3.	About some technical details. Probably I have missed something, but based on the description, the definition of the k-order adjacency matrix is not clear. Does k refer to the shortest path from i to j? Or is it a parameter that varies with the number of layers l? Could you explain why you average the power series? Why does this incorporate more shallow layer information to reduce the risk of over-smoothing?
4.	The writing of this paper can be improved. Figure 2 is not cited. How the input of MLP is aggregated from low-frequency and high-frequency signals is not clear.
content.summary_of_the_review: The motivation of the paper is meaningful and insightful. Theoretical proofs of Frequency Principle on Graph Network and effectiveness of dropout are significant and novel, which I think are the main contributions of this paper. However, the architecture of the proposed model does not contain a special mechanism to solve the problems raised, though improved performance on node classification tasks.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2212 by Reviewer 3k2q

content.summary_of_the_paper: Recent papers in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have looked at how to effectively leverage high frequency signals from node features in various ways. In that line of work, this paper proposes to decompose the node features into high frequency and low frequency components. These components are then propagated over the graph and then fed to a neural network for class prediction. The individual neural networks are regularized such that all the networks produce similar logits.
content.main_review:
While the idea of directly decomposing node features into respective low and high frequency components is interesting, there are five problems with the paper as presented: 1] Lack of clarity, 2] Incremental Novelty 3] Errors and Typos 4] Missing baseline 5] More datasets

The following paragraphs will expand on these a little more,
1. **Lack of Clarity:** Several aspects of the paper are quite unclear from the reading. **A]** The paper proposes to use Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) on the node feature matrix to get the low and high frequency components. It is unclear how this is actually done. DWTs are usually applied to 1-D data like time-varying signals or 2-D data like images, in both these cases, the positional information is important. However, in the node feature matrix, we can permute the node-rows of the matrix (as long as we permute the corresponding rows and columns of the graph as well) and we can permute the feature-columns, since we treat them as bags of nodes and features and their ordering is arbitrary. Thus it is unclear how the DWT is performed on the node feature matrix. Is it independent of these permutations? If not, are the authors performing some sort of ordering on the matrix prior to computing the DWT? And if the DWT is not independent of permutation then what do the low and high frequency components mean in that case. **B]**  In Figure 3a and 3b, it is unclear what Shallow and Deep GCNs mean given that in both figures the number of layers are being varied. **C]** When the dropout is performed, is the bernoulli sampling done independently for the various low/high frequency components or the sampling done for each node and all the corresponding low and high frequency components for that particular node are then dropped? The paper makes a statement *Under the homophily assumption, this strategy is interpretable. Each node that is randomly mixed with information from its neighbors is an approximate representation of their original low-frequency and high-frequency features.* Why is the homophily assumption important for this statement? Isn't it true in general? **D]** Why is the final loss term defined in two parts supervised and consistency loss? Why not use feature pooling methods? What are the merits of the proposed method over feature pooling approaches? **E]** The complexity analysis does not talk about the cost of doing wavelet decomposition of the node feature matrix? How expensive is this decomposition for sparse/dense matrices? **F]** Are there references for Proposition 1? **G]** How does lower dim leads to lower d_M? What does it mean when it is said, *the propagation on low-frequency feature is more easily tend to subspace M* ? **H]** Proof of Theorem 2 does not follow easily. It would be better to write out a complete proof with full details.

2. **Incremental Novelty:** Much of the proposed approach is just directly taken from [Feng et. al] with some modifications.

3. **Errors and Typos:** The paper has quite a few typos, errors and missing notation explanations. **A]** Does the title meant to say "affect" instead of "effect"? **B]** Y-axis label in Figure 1? **C]** What is GRAND in Section 1 Paragraph 5? It appears without explanation. **D]** Strange citation in Section 2, Paragraph 1, Line 2 "wan" **E]** "Studing" --> "Studies" Section 2, Paragraph 4, Line 1 **F]** A paper should be self contained. In Section 4.3, even if taking notation from another paper, it is better to write out the definition in the paper itself, so that one does not have to switch between two papers to understand notations. Additionally, I would caution the authors to not lift statements verbatim from other papers.

4. **Missing baseline:** Apart from FAGCN and UFGConv, another approach that has proposed to leverage low and high frequency signals from node features is GPRGNN [Chien et. al] which is missing from baseline comparisons.

5. **More datasets:** Given the simplicity of the proposed approach, the experiments could have been performed on a some more datasets. There are few more datasets listed in [Chien et. al]. Additionally, another experiment on large dataset could have also been done to strengthen the paper.

In light of the above issues, I am inclined to reject the paper.

**References:**

Wenzheng Feng, Jie Zhang, Yuxiao Dong, Yu Han, Huanbo Luan, Qian Xu, Qiang Yang, Evgeny Kharlamov, and Jie Tang. Graph random neural networks for semi-supervised learning on graphs. NIPS, 2020.

Eli Chien, Jianhao Peng, Pan Li and Olgica Milenkovic. Adaptive Universal Generalized PageRank Graph Neural Network. ICLR, 2021.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors try to introduce notions from frequency analysis in Graph Neural Networks. In particular, they decompose the input features into low-frequency and high-frequency components, using wavelets theory, and they show that low-frequency signals can be learned faster in GCNs. Based on that observation, they propose a new type of architecture i.e., Multi-Scale Frequency Enhanced Graph Neural Networks (MSF-GNNs) which considers multi-scale representations from wavelet decomposition. They verify the performance in classical node classification datasets.
content.main_review:
I believe that the paper could be improved in the following aspects. 

1) The motivation of adopting the frequency decomposition in not clear. That is the main novelty of the paper, but at the same time, it raises many questions. Frequency decomposition in the feature space, ignores completely the graph structure, while the main assumption of the graph-based representation learning is that the signals/features depend on the topology. Could you please justify that choice? What happens  if we reorder the nodes of the graph? The frequency decomposition will be completely different. Can the authors comment on that? 

2)  The low frequency/high frequency behaviour is investigated only on GCNs. Does it hold for other architectures as well?

3) Fig. 1 is not very informative. Please clarify. 

4) Non-linearities are removed also in Simplified Graph Convolution Networks.  

5) Please discuss T.  

6) Where does Proposition 1 come from? Please explain. 

7) GAT is not based on graph convolution in the Fourier domain. Please check (p.3-related work).

8) Please add a reference for db2 wavelets. 

9) Please update the references carefully and make them consistent. 

10) The paper is very quickly written. There are terminologies that are used but are never defined. Different typos exist int he text.
   - p2: What is GRAND?
   - p3: Related work section: Graph Neural Networks: "to the Graph"; Is there a reason why Graph is capital?
   - p3: Related work section: Graph Neural Networks: "cannot fully exploit" instead of "cannot fully exploiting"
   - p3: Please rephrase the sentence: "Here, consider a node classification task, the goal is to predict..."
   - p4: Figure 2 is never referred in the text. 
   - p4: Section 4: Please specify in which dimension the wavelet decomposition if performed (M or N)
   - p4: Figure 3 is not clear. Please give details on the setup.
   - p4: many sentences start with "And". Please rephrase. 
   - p5: "we randomly dropping" please correct. 
   - p5: Define \bar{X} 
   - p6: Eq. 3: m is s? Please correct. 
   - p6: "Considering 2 representations" substitute "2" with "two" 
   - p6: "my model"? Please correct. 
   - p6: 'Depend on their different performances" replace with 'Depending ...."
   - p7: "is more easily tend to..." please correct. 
   - p8: "a similar classification results" replace with "similar classification results"
   - p13: "which adopted" replace with "which were adopted"
   - p13: "and the for each node": please fix.
content.summary_of_the_review:
To summarise, the paper lacks in terms of:
- a solid motivation of the proposed approach, and a better positioning with respect to the state of the art (especially multi-scale representations that take into account the graph structure). This part is only superficially treated. 
- clarity in the text.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a Multi-Scale Frequency enhanced framework for GNNs (MSF-GNNs). They firstly decompose the original features of nodes into different frequencies, and then reuse them as the new features.
content.main_review:
This paper proposes a Multi-Scale Frequency enhanced framework for GNNs (MSF-GNNs). They firstly decompose the original features of nodes into different frequencies, and then reuse them as the new features. Unfortunately, this framework is based on the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) in the Euclidean space, which is unsuitable for the graph domain. Besides, I also have many concerns about the detailed steps, the design of the framework, and the theoretical proofs of the theorems.

Comments:
1. As stated above, I am afraid it is not proper to use the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), a frequency analysis tool in the Euclidean space, since both the node and feature dimensions are permutation invariant for the node feature matrix of these three citation networks. 
2. In Sec. 3, I am afraid that the final output of GCN is not Z = H^{(2)}.
3. In the hat of Sec. 4, I am wondering what the shape of every X^{*}, why there is only one component for low-frequency but n components for high-frequency, and what n is.
4. In Fig. 3, I am afraid that the number of layers should not have the decimals. 
5. In Sec. 4.1, I am afraid that the necessity of information propagation is not clear. 
6. In Sec. 4.1, I am wondering what the operation {…} means. (H^{(0)}={, ,…,})
7. In Sec. 4.2, I am wondering why to use every Z^{s} to get the prediction instead of adding them up.
8. In Def. 1, I am wondering why \mathcal{M} is defined an M-dimensional subspace instead of MxC-dim, and what the Geometric Interpretation of this "subspace". 
9. The proofs of Proposition 1 and Lemma 1 are missing.
10. In Lemma 1, I am afraid that the "reversible" matrix is always square.
11. In Theorem 1, I am afraid that \hat{A} maybe not reversible.
12. In experiments, I am afraid that the experiments rely on Cora, Citeseer, and PubMed results. However, these benchmarks are known to be oversaturated and unreliable as graph representation learning benchmarks (see e.g., "Pitfalls of Graph Neural Network Evaluation" from Shchur et al.). The paper may better report the results on either OGB (Hu et al., NeurIPS'20) or Benchmarking-GNNs (Dwivedi et al.).
content.summary_of_the_review: Unfortunately, this framework is based on the Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) in the Euclidean space, which is unsuitable for the graph domain. Besides, I also have many concerns about the detailed steps, the design of the framework, and the theoretical proofs of the theorems.
